categories.name: Technology & IP
categories.description: Protection of creative works, patents, AI ethics, and data privacy.
categories.descriptionHtml:
Technology and intellectual property law covers how creative works, brands, inventions, and personal data are legally protected — and each of those protections works differently, has its own registration process (or none at all), and lasts for a different length of time. This hub explains the basics and the areas where jurisdiction makes the biggest difference. It is general information, not legal advice.

Trademarks, Copyright, and Patents Are Not Interchangeable

A trademark protects brand identifiers — names, logos, slogans — used in commerce and can, in principle, last indefinitely as long as it's used and renewed. Copyright protects original creative expression (writing, code, art, music) automatically from the moment it's fixed in a tangible form, without registration, though registration adds real legal benefits in the U.S. A patent protects a new, useful, non-obvious invention, but only after a formal application and examination process, and only for a limited term. Confusing the three — for example, assuming copyright covers a business name, which is really a trademark question — is one of the most common mistakes founders make. See our guides on trademark vs. copyright and what a patent is and how to get one.

Data Privacy Law

Any business collecting personal data from users now has to think about which privacy regime applies — the EU's GDPR, California's CCPA/CPRA, or another jurisdiction's law entirely — and these regimes don't all define terms like personal data, controller, and processor the same way, or impose the same obligations. Our guide on data privacy law basics walks through the core concepts a business needs before it can even evaluate compliance.

Why Jurisdiction Matters Especially Here

Technology and IP law is one of the areas where jurisdiction matters most, precisely because digital products and services routinely reach users in multiple countries at once. The UK's post-Brexit UK GDPR and the EU's GDPR started from the same text but have since diverged in specific ways — a good example of how the same law can mean two different compliance obligations depending on which regulator has jurisdiction. See our guide on UK GDPR vs. EU GDPR.

Key Terms

IP (intellectual property) — the umbrella term for trademarks, copyright, patents, and trade secrets. Prior art — existing knowledge or inventions a patent examiner checks a new application against. Fair use — a U.S. copyright doctrine allowing limited use of protected work without permission in certain circumstances. Data controller / processor — under GDPR-style laws, the entity that decides how personal data is used versus the entity that processes it on the controller's behalf.

Related Legal Areas

Contract and formation questions that often come up alongside IP protection — like how startups structure ownership and agreements — are covered in our Business & Corporate hub.

Authoritative Sources & Further Reading

  • United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) — official source for U.S. patent and trademark filing and search.
  • U.S. Copyright Office — copyright registration and official guidance.
  • Federal Trade Commission — Consumer Privacy — U.S. privacy enforcement guidance for businesses.
  • European Commission — Data Protection — the EU's official GDPR legal framework resource.
